theta1Deg_desc: Angle of incident laser beam relative to the surface normal in degrees
n1_desc: Refractive index of top medium of incidence
n2_desc: Refractive index of bottom refracting medium
wavelength_desc: Laser beam wavelength in nanometers (visible spectrum 380 to 750 nm)
laserPower_desc: Incident laser beam power in milliwatts
real_dispersion_effect: In real mode, Cauchy chromatic dispersion slightly alters refractive index across wavelengths, fanning white light into a rainbow spectrum
preset_glass_to_air_tir: Glass to Air Total Internal Reflection (TIR)
formula_reflection_desc: The angle of the reflected ray with the normal always equals the angle of incidence: θr = θi
formula_snell_desc: The product of index and sine of angle is conserved across optical boundaries: n1 sin(θ1) = n2 sin(θ2)
formula_critical_desc: When light travels from denser to rarer medium (n1 > n2), light reflects 100% internally beyond the critical angle
formula_brewster_desc: At this incident angle, reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, making reflected light 100% linear s-polarized
formula_fresnel_desc: Governs electromagnetic wave power division between reflected and transmitted beams as a function of incidence angle and polarization
theoryTitle: Physics of Light Refraction, Snell's Law & Fresnel Coefficients
theoryP1: When a light ray strikes the boundary between two transparent media with differing refractive indices, part of its radiant energy is reflected according to the Law of Reflection, and part enters the second medium with altered velocity and propagation direction. According to Fermat's Principle of Least Time, light traverses the path that minimizes travel time, which yields Snell's Law: n₁ sin(θ₁) = n₂ sin(θ₂).
theoryP2: The speed of light in any medium is inversely proportional to its refractive index (v = c/n). Entering a denser medium (n₁ < n₂), the refracted ray bends toward the surface normal (θ₂ < θ₁). Conversely, exiting into a rarer medium (n₁ > n₂), light bends away from the normal. At the critical angle θ_c = arcsin(n₂/n₁), the angle of refraction reaches 90°; beyond this angle, total internal reflection occurs, preventing any light from escaping.
theoryP3: Fresnel's equations determine the partition of optical power for transverse electric (s) and transverse magnetic (p) polarization modes. At Brewster's angle (tan θ_B = n₂/n₁), the p-polarized reflectance vanishes completely, yielding a purely polarized reflected ray.
